title: Log first, then crash and replay

steps.say: Client sets A=90. Page 7 changes only in memory, so it is dirty. The copy on disk still says A=100.
Before anything else, the change goes into the log as LSN 41 (A: 100 to 90). One sequential append, no random write.
Commit adds LSN 42 and forces the log to disk (fsync). Only then does the client get OK. Page 7 on disk is still old, and that is fine.
Another transaction sets B=9 (LSN 43). It has not committed yet.
Power cut. Memory is wiped, with both dirty pages. Disk still holds A=100 and B=5. The log holds LSN 41 to 43.
On restart we read the log from the start. LSN 41 was committed but never reached the data file, so we redo it. Page 7 becomes A=90.
LSN 43 has no commit record after it, so we skip it. B stays 5. No half-done transaction appears.
A checkpoint notes that page 7 is safe on disk, so the log up to LSN 42 can be deleted. This keeps the next recovery short.

title: Writes go to memory, then sorted files

steps.say: Client writes k5=a and k2=b. They go into the memtable, a sorted structure in memory, and into the WAL for safety. No disk seek.
Two more writes: k9 and k8. The memtable now holds 4 keys, which is our limit here. Real limit is about 64 MB.
Flush: the memtable is written as one sorted file, sst1, in a single sequential write. Files are never edited after this.
More writes follow and make sst2. Key k5 now exists twice: old value a in sst1, new value c in sst2.
Read k5: check memtable, then newest file first. sst2 has it, so the answer is c and we stop early.
Read k4, a key that does not exist: we must look in the memtable and every file. This is read amplification. With 10 files, it is 10 lookups.
Compaction merges sst1 and sst2 like merge sort. For k5 it keeps c and drops the old a.

add.label: L1 merged
add.sub: k1 k2 k3 k5=c k7 k8 k9

steps.say: The two small files are deleted. Reads now check one file. The price: these bytes were written again, so each byte can be rewritten about 10 times as it moves down levels.

title: Insert that splits a full page

groups.label: B-tree on disk, 4 keys per page

steps.say: Look up key 45: read the root, then leaf B. Two page reads for any key. With 500 keys per page, 4 levels cover about 60 billion keys.
Insert key 22. It belongs in leaf A, but A already has 4 keys: 10 15 20 25. Adding one more will not fit.
Splitting touches 3 pages, so we log it first. If we crash in the middle, the log can finish the job.

add.label: LOG: split A, 22 to A2, parent +22

steps.say: Split: A keeps 10 15 20. A new page A2 gets 22 25. Each is half full, so there is room to grow.
Crash now, before the parent is updated. The root still says [30|60], so a lookup for 22 goes to leaf A and does not find it.
On restart the log is replayed. The parent gets the new separator key 22 and now points to A2.
Lookup 22 now works: root, then A2. If the root were full, it would split too, and the tree would grow one level.
Cost: a 16-byte insert rewrote whole 4 KB pages (A, A2, root). That is write amplification, the price of fast sorted reads.

title: Readers never block writers

steps.say: T20 starts and reads the account. It sees v1: balance 100, created by T10.
T25 updates the balance to 70. It does not overwrite. It writes a new version v2 and marks v1 as ended by T25.
T20 reads again. T25 has not committed, so T20 still sees v1 = 100. No lock, no waiting.
T25 commits. Version v2 is now visible to any transaction that starts after this.
T20 is still running with its old snapshot, so it reads 100 again (repeatable read). New transaction T30 reads v2 = 70.
T30 updates twice more, making v3 and v4. T20 may still need v1, so old versions pile up. This is table bloat.
T20 finally ends. Vacuum finds that no transaction needs v1 and v2 and frees them. One transaction left open for hours would have blocked this cleanup.

title: Two transactions race on one row

steps.say: Both transactions read row X: stock=5, version 7. Nobody takes a lock.
Each works on its own private copy. T1 wants to sell 1 (stock 4). T2 wants to sell 2 (stock 3).
T1 tries to commit: 'apply only if X is still version 7'. It is, so the commit succeeds and X becomes version 8.
T2 tries the same check, but X is now version 8. The check fails: a conflict.
T2's work is thrown away. This is the cost of OCC: wasted work when someone else wins.
T2 retries. It reads again and gets stock=4, version 8, then computes stock=2.
This time the version still matches, so T2 commits. X becomes version 9.
With one hot row, it gets worse: with 10 transactions at once, 9 lose in round one, 8 in round two, and so on. OCC is great when conflicts are rare, bad when they are common.

title: Write skew under snapshot isolation

groups.label: Table on_call (rule: at least 1 doctor on call)

steps.say: Alice and Bob both feel ill and each starts a transaction at the same moment. Each gets a snapshot where 2 doctors are on call.
Each checks the rule: 2 on call, so one can leave. Both decide it is safe.
T1 sets Alice to off call.
T2 sets Bob to off call. T1 wrote Alice's row and T2 wrote Bob's row, so the database sees no write conflict.
Both commit successfully. Now 0 doctors are on call. Each transaction was correct alone, but together they broke the rule. This is write skew.
Run again with SERIALIZABLE isolation. Same start: both see 2 on call, and T1 commits first.
T2 tries to commit. The database notices T1 changed data that T2 had read (the count). T2's decision is no longer valid.
T2 retries and now sees only 1 on call. It refuses to leave. The rule holds. Cost: some transactions abort, and the app must retry.

title: Crash recovery in three passes

steps.say: T1 changed page 5 (not yet flushed) and committed. T2 changed page 6 and the buffer pool flushed it early, before T2 committed. Now the power fails.
Pass 1, analysis: read the log from the last checkpoint. T1 has a COMMIT, so it is a winner. T2 has none, so it is a loser.
Pass 2, redo: replay history. Page 5 has pageLSN 0, less than 10, so redo LSN 10. Page 5 now has T1's change.
LSN 11: page 6 already has pageLSN 11, so the change is already there. Skip it. Page LSNs stop us from applying a change twice.
Pass 3, undo: T2 never committed, so its change on page 6 must go. We reverse it.
The undo is logged as a compensation record (CLR). If we crash again during recovery, we will not undo the same change twice.
Page 6 is clean and the database opens. Recovery time depends on how much log came after the last checkpoint.
Cost: with a checkpoint every 30 s, replay takes a few seconds. With no checkpoint for an hour, replay can take minutes.

add.label: Replay time ~ log since last checkpoint

title: Compaction and a deleted key

steps.say: The user deleted k3. A delete is written as a marker (tombstone) in file a. The old values of k3 are still in files b, c and d. The key is stored 4 times.
Reading k5 has to look in file a, then file b. Level 0 files overlap, so every one must be checked. Too many L0 files make reads slow.
L0 has 2 files, which is the trigger. Compaction picks both, plus file c from L1 because its keys overlap.
Merge the three sorted files into one new file m. For k3 only the newest entry survives: the tombstone.
The tombstone must stay. File d at Level 2 still holds k3=v, and without the marker the deleted value would come back to life.
Old inputs a, b, c are deleted. We read 7 entries and wrote 5, and this work repeats at every level: that is write amplification.
Later m is merged with file d at the bottom level. Nothing is below, so the tombstone and k3=v are dropped together. Space is finally freed.
Result: k3 is gone completely. Disk space from a delete came back only after two compactions, so a delete-heavy table can use much more disk than its live data.

title: Copy on write vs merge on read

steps.say: UPDATE row 7 (change one value). Two table styles handle this very differently. First: copy on write (COW).
COW rewrites the whole file: read all 128 MB, change one row, write 128 MB to a new file. One row changed, 128 MB written.
The old file is removed. A query reads one clean file and needs no merging. COW is slow to write but fast to read.
Now merge on read (MOR). The same kind of update writes only a small delta file: row 7 has the new value, 1 KB.
A query must read the big file and the delta, then merge them. Writes became 100,000 times smaller, and reads do extra work.
Updates continue and deltas pile up: delta-2, delta-3. Each read merges more sources, so reads get slower and slower.
Compaction folds all deltas into the base file in the background. Reads are fast again. MOR moves cost from write time to read time and compaction time.

title: Delete without rewriting the file

steps.say: part-001.parquet holds 5 rows, ids 1 to 5 (real files hold millions). We run DELETE WHERE id=3.
Rewriting the file just to drop one row would copy everything. Instead we write the row position into a small delete vector: bit 2.
A query reads the tiny delete vector first, then scans the file.
The row at position 2 is skipped. The result is 1, 2, 4, 5. The data file did not change at all.
More deletes (id 1, id 5) only flip more bits. Each delete costs a few bytes, not a file rewrite.
Cost: 3 of 5 rows are dead, but every query still reads the whole file and drops 60% of it. With 90% deleted, this wastes most of the I/O.
A maintenance job rewrites the file with only live rows into part-002.parquet and drops the delete vector.
Now the query reads 2 rows and the vector is empty. Deletes are cheap now and cleaned up later.

title: Skipping files with min/max

groups.label: Files and their footers (min/max of price)

steps.say: A query wants rows with price > 900. Each 100 MB file stores min and max price in its footer, so we can look there first.
The data was written in arrival order, so every file holds a mix of cheap and expensive items. All four files have max above 900.
No file can be ruled out, so all four are read: 400 MB scanned to find a few hundred rows. The zone map did not help.
Rewrite the table sorted by price (clustering). Now each file covers one price range.
Same query. Files 1, 2 and 3 have max below 900, so they cannot contain a match. We skip them using only the footers.
Only file 4 is read: 100 MB instead of 400 MB, four times less I/O.
The limit: min/max says only 'maybe'. File 4 spans 801 to 995, so most of its rows are still below 900 and we scan it all. Zone maps help only when the data is sorted on that column.

title: Reading one column of three

groups.label: Row store: each page holds whole rows
Column store: one file per column

actors.label: country.col
actors.sub: IN US IN DE US IN

steps.say: The table has 3 columns (id, country, amount) and 3 million rows. We want only SUM(amount).
Row store: amounts sit inside whole rows, so we must read every page. 300 MB are read to use 100 MB of amounts.
Column store: all amounts are stored together. We read amount.col only. id.col and country.col are never touched: 100 MB.
Similar values sit side by side, so they compress well. country.col becomes a dictionary (IN=0, US=1, DE=2) and small numbers. amount.col drops from 100 MB to about 25 MB.
The sum runs as one tight loop over an array of numbers, which the CPU does very fast. Total: about 0.1 s.
The cost: one INSERT must update every column file. A row store changes 1 page; this table changes 3 files.
So column stores batch many rows into one big write. They are great for analytics (read few columns, many rows) and poor for single-row updates.

title: Building and querying a word index

groups.label: Inverted index: word to list of document ids

steps.say: We have 3 documents. A scan for 'red fox' would read all of them. With 100 million documents that is far too slow.
Index doc 1: split the text into words and add doc 1 to each word's list (the posting list).
Index doc 2: 'red' gets a second entry, and 'car' is a new word.
Index doc 3: 'fox' gets doc 3, 'car' gets doc 3. Lists stay sorted by id.
Query 'red AND fox'. We look up each word directly. No document is read yet.
Merge the two sorted lists: {1, 2} and {1, 3} share only doc 1. Cost depends on list length, not on the number of documents.
Problem case: a common word. 'the' appears in 90 million of 100 million documents, so its list is huge. 'the AND fox' must walk a 90-million-entry list.
Fix: start from the shortest list ('fox', 2 ids) and jump through the long one with skip pointers. Search engines also drop very common words or score them low.

title: Hash join and what happens when it spills

steps.say: Join orders with users on user id. Step one: read the small table and put each user in a hash table in memory, keyed by user id.
Step two: stream the big table one row at a time. Order 1 has user=2. One hash lookup finds Ben, and we output (Ben, $40).
Order 2 has user=9. The lookup finds nothing, so the row is dropped. The big table is read once and never sorted.
Order 3 has user=1, which finds Ana. Output grows to 2 rows. Total cost: one pass over each table.
Failure case: the 'small' table is really 20 GB, but the hash table has only 4 GB of memory. The hash table no longer fits.
The join spills: both tables are split by hash into 8 partitions and written to disk. Each partition pair is joined alone. Every byte is now written and read again, about 3 times the I/O.
Fix: the optimizer picks the smaller input as the build side, filters it first, or sends the small table to every worker (broadcast). If both are big, it uses a sort-merge join instead.

title: Shuffle and a skewed key

groups.label: Map side: read and group by country
Shuffle files on disk (one per mapper)
Reduce side: one partition per reducer

steps.say: Each mapper reads its own piece of the orders table. Most rows (70%) have country = US.
Each mapper hashes the key (country) and splits its rows into 3 groups. It writes them to one local file. hash(US) mod 3 = 1, so every US row goes to group 1.
Now the shuffle: each reducer fetches its group from all 3 files over the network. Same key always lands on the same reducer.
The skew shows up: reducer 1 got every US row, 900 MB. The others got 10 MB (reducer 0) and 90 MB (reducer 2).
Reducers 0 and 2 finish in 3 seconds and sit idle. Reducer 1 needs 60 seconds and may run out of memory. The whole stage takes as long as its slowest task.
Fix: salting. Add a random suffix to the hot key: US_0, US_1, US_2. Now the US rows spread over all reducers, 300 MB each.
A second small step adds the three partial sums into one US total. The stage now takes about 20 s instead of 60 s, at the price of an extra step.

title: Re-planning a query while it runs

groups.label: Plan made before the run (from guessed sizes)

steps.say: The planner has only old table statistics. It guesses users = 2 GB, too big to broadcast, so it plans a sort-merge join: shuffle both sides into 200 partitions.
Stage 1 runs: scan users with the filter country = 'IN'. The real result is only 8 MB, not 2 GB.
AQE sees 8 MB, below the 10 MB broadcast limit. It drops the sort-merge join and plans a broadcast join: send the 8 MB to every worker. The 50 GB orders table is never shuffled.
Next, an aggregation made 200 shuffle partitions of only 0.5 MB each. 200 tiny tasks waste more time starting than working. AQE merges them into 5 tasks of about 20 MB.
Then it finds a skewed partition: one holds 4 GB while the median is 40 MB. AQE splits it into 40 pieces of 100 MB, so no single task runs for minutes.
Result: the query that took 12 minutes with the first plan finishes in about 3 minutes, using real sizes instead of guesses.
The limit: AQE can only change what has not started. Stage 1 ran on the old plan, and facts appear only after a shuffle finishes. A bad first stage cannot be undone.

title: One row at a time, pulled by next()

groups.label: Operators: each calls next() on the one below

steps.say: The top operator asks for a row: next(). Project asks Filter, Filter asks Scan. Nothing moves until someone asks.
Scan reads the first row (1, 50) and hands it up.
50 is more than 10, so Filter passes the row up. Project keeps only the id and puts it in the output.
The user asks for more. Project calls next() again. Scan returns (2, 5), and Filter rejects it because 5 is not above 10.
Filter asks Scan again on its own. Scan returns (3, 70), which passes. The output now has 1 and 3.
Last row (4, 3) is rejected too. Scan then answers end of data and the end signal travels up through every operator.
Cost: 4 rows needed about 12 function calls. At 1 billion rows with 3 operators that is billions of calls, each with a virtual jump that stalls the CPU.

title: The same query, 1,024 rows at a time

steps.say: Same query, new idea: each next() returns a batch of 1,024 rows, not one row. Project asks Filter, Filter asks Scan, once.
Scan returns the amount column for rows 1 to 1,024 as a plain array of numbers.
Filter runs one tight loop over the array: is each value above 10? The CPU can test 8 values in one SIMD instruction, and the array sits in cache.
The result is a selection vector: positions 0, 2, ... that passed. The data is not copied, only the list of survivors moves on.
Project takes the id column for those positions and writes the output. Total: 3 next() calls for 1,024 rows. The row-at-a-time engine needed about 3,000.
Cost case: a very selective filter passes only 3 of 1,024 rows. Later operators now get nearly empty batches and lose the benefit, so engines compact batches or fuse operators.
It also needs column-friendly data, such as Parquet. Most modern engines (DuckDB, Photon, ClickHouse) use batches for this reason.

title: Reading the database log as a stream

steps.say: The app inserts order 7 for $40. The database appends the change to its write-ahead log. This log exists anyway, for crash recovery.
Two more changes arrive: id=7 goes to $55 (LSN 101), then id=7 is deleted (LSN 102). The log keeps every step in order.
The connector tails the log like tail -f. It reads LSN 100 without querying the table, so the app sees no extra load. It remembers its offset.
It publishes the change as an event to the Kafka topic, keyed by id=7 so all events for one order stay in order.
The connector moves on and publishes the update and the delete as well.
A consumer applies the events in order. The index shows $40, then $55, then the row is removed. The copy follows the database within seconds.
Failure: the connector crashes after publishing LSN 101 but before saving its offset. The DB must keep log files until the connector returns, so disk can fill up.
On restart it resumes from the saved offset and publishes the update (LSN 101) again. This is at-least-once delivery. The consumer ignores it, because it has already applied LSN 101 for key 7.

title: A partition log, replicas and consumers

steps.say: A producer sends order events to partition 0. The leader appends each to the end of the log and gives it the next offset. Offset 0 is 'click'.
Offsets 1 and 2 follow: 'cart' and 'pay'. The log is never edited, only appended, which is a fast sequential write.
The follower broker copies the log, in the same order, and acknowledges. Now two machines hold offsets 0 to 2.
Consumer A reads from offset 0. It tracks its own position. Reading does not remove anything.
Consumer B starts later from offset 0 and reads the same events at its own speed. One log, many independent readers.
The producer sends offset 3 'ship' with acks=1: the leader says OK before the follower has copied it.
The leader machine dies. Offset 3 existed only there, so it is lost, even though the producer was told OK. The follower holds offsets 0 to 2.
The follower becomes the new leader. Consumers continue from their saved offsets. With acks=all the leader waits for the follower, so offset 3 would have been safe.
